translation_en: Abu Hurairah reported that a man said to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: “My father died leaving property but no will. Will it expiate for him if I give charity on his behalf?” The Prophet said, “Yes.” The chain includes Yahya ibn Ayyub, Qutaybah ibn Said, Ali ibn Hujr, Ismail ibn Jafar, al-Ala, his father, and Abu Hurairah.

Abu Hurairah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “When a person dies, his deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge from which people benefit, or a righteous child who prays for him.” The transmitters are Yahya ibn Ayyub, Qutaybah ibn Said, Ibn Hujr, Ismail ibn Jafar, al-Ala, his father, and Abu Hurairah.

Ibn Umar reported that Umar acquired land at Khaybar and asked the Prophet what to do, saying he had never obtained wealth more precious to him. The Prophet said, “If you wish, keep its principal intact and give its produce in charity.” Umar made it an endowment: it could not be sold, bought, inherited, or given away. He gave its proceeds to the poor, relatives, emancipation of slaves, the path of Allah, travelers, and guests. Its caretaker could eat from it reasonably or feed a friend, without taking wealth for himself. The account also notes a wording variation: “without accumulating wealth.” Umar also directed the endowment income to the poor, relatives, freeing slaves, the path of Allah, travelers, and guests. Its administrator could eat from it reasonably or feed a friend without taking wealth for himself. The later wording is explained as not accumulating wealth.

This is the same endowment report from Ibn Umar through several chains. Ibn Abi Zaidah’s and Azhar’s versions end with permission for the caretaker to feed a friend without taking personal wealth; they omit the later wording discussion. Ibn Abi Adi’s version includes Sulaym’s account of reporting the hadith to Muhammad and their discussion of the wording.

Umar said he acquired land at Khaybar that he valued above any property he had owned. He asked the Messenger of Allah about it, and the Prophet gave the same instruction as in the preceding report. This chain is Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, Abu Dawud al-Hafari, Umar ibn Sad, Sufyan, Ibn Awn, Nafi, Ibn Umar, and Umar; it omits the later wording discussion.

Talhah ibn Musarrif said: “I asked Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa whether the Messenger of Allah made a will.” He said no. I asked why Muslims were instructed to make wills. He replied, “He enjoined the Book of Allah.” The chain includes Yahya ibn Yahya, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, Malik ibn Mighwal, and Talhah.

This is the same account through Waki and Ibn Numayr from Malik ibn Mighwal. Waki’s version asks how people were instructed to make a will; Ibn Numayr’s asks how the will was prescribed for Muslims. The reports have the same chain and meaning, but Waki wording asks how people were ordered to make a will, while Ibn Numayr asks how the will was prescribed for Muslims.

Aishah said: “The Messenger of Allah left no dinar, dirham, sheep, or camel, and he did not make a will.” This is reported through al-Amash, Abu Wail, Masruq, and Aishah, by Abd Allah ibn Numayr and Abu Muawiyah. Aishah reported this through Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah and Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Numayr, from Abd Allah ibn Numayr, Abu Muawiyah, al-Amash, Abu Wail, and Masruq.
This is the same report from Aishah through al-Amash, with another chain: Zuhayr ibn Harb, Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, and Ali ibn Khashram transmit it through Jarir or Isa ibn Yunus.

Al-Aswad ibn Yazid said that people mentioned to Aishah that Ali had been appointed to make the Prophet’s will. She asked, “When did he make that will? I was leaning him against my chest—or she said, in my lap—and he called for a basin. He then slumped into my lap, and I did not realize he had died. So when did he make a will to Ali?”

Ibn Abbas said: “Thursday! And what a Thursday!” Then he wept until his tears soaked the pebbles. Asked what happened on Thursday, he said the Messenger of Allah’s illness became severe. The Prophet said, “Bring me something to write with, so I can write a document for you after which you will not go astray.” They disputed, though no one should dispute in a Prophet’s presence. Some asked whether he was delirious and said to question him. The Prophet said, “Leave me; what I am experiencing is better. I advise you of three things: expel the polytheists from the Arabian Peninsula, receive delegations with the same hospitality I used to give them,” and he was silent about the third, or Ibn Abbas said he forgot it. This is also transmitted through al-Hasan ibn Bishr from Sufyan.

Ibn Abbas said: “Thursday! And what a Thursday!” His tears flowed until they looked like a string of pearls on his cheeks. The Messenger of Allah said, “Bring me a shoulder blade and ink—or a tablet and ink—so I can write you a document after which you will never go astray.” They said, “The Messenger of Allah is delirious.” Ibn Abbas said his tears ran down his cheeks like a string of pearls. The Prophet asked for a shoulder blade and ink, or a tablet and ink, so that he could write a document after which they would never go astray. Those present said the Messenger was delirious.

Ibn Abbas reported that when the Messenger of Allah was near death, with Umar ibn al-Khattab and other men in the house, he said, “Come, let me write you a document after which you will not go astray.” Umar said the Prophet’s pain had overcome him and that they had the Quran, which was sufficient as Allah’s Book. The people in the house disagreed and argued. Some urged them to bring the writing materials so the Messenger could write; others agreed with Umar. When they argued loudly in the Prophet’s presence, he said, “Get up.” Ibn Abbas used to say that the greatest calamity was the dispute and noise that came between the Messenger and writing that document for them. Ibn Abbas said that, as the Messenger of Allah was near death, Umar and other men were in the house. The Prophet asked them to bring writing materials so he could write a document after which they would not go astray. Umar said the Prophet was overwhelmed by pain and that the Quran was sufficient. The household then disagreed: some wanted to bring the materials, while others supported Umar. When their argument and noise became excessive in the Prophet’s presence, he told them to get up. Ibn Abbas used to say that the greatest calamity was their dispute and noise preventing the Messenger from writing that document. The report is transmitted by Muhammad ibn Rafi and Abd ibn Humayd from Abd al-Razzaq, Maamar, al-Zuhri, and Ubayd Allah ibn Abdullah ibn Utbah.

This is the same report from Ibn Abbas through several chains from al-Zuhri, including Malik, Ibn Uyaynah, Yunus, Maamar, and Hisham ibn Urwah from Bakr ibn Wail, with the chain and meaning of al-Layth’s narration. The chain is Yahya ibn Yahya and Muhammad ibn Rumh from al-Layth, and Qutaybah from Layth, through Ibn Shihab, Ubayd Allah ibn Abdullah, and Ibn Abbas.

Abdullah ibn Umar reported that the Messenger of Allah one day prohibited vows, saying: “A vow does not change anything; it only extracts something from a miser.” The chain is Zuhayr ibn Harb and Ishaq ibn Ibrahim from Jarir, Mansur, Abdullah ibn Murrah, and Ibn Umar. The same ruling is reported through Malik, Ibn Uyaynah, Ibn Wahb and Yunus, Abd al-Razzaq and Maamar, and Abdah ibn Sulayman from Hisham ibn Urwah and Bakr ibn Wail, all from al-Zuhri, with the chain and meaning of al-Layth narration.

Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet said: “A vow neither brings anything forward nor delays it; it only draws something out of a miser.” The chain is Zuhayr ibn Harb and Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, from Jarir, Mansur, and Abdullah ibn Murrah, reporting from Abdullah ibn Umar.

Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet prohibited vows and said: “They bring no good; they only draw something out of a miser.” This is transmitted through Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna from Shubah, Mansur, and Abdullah ibn Murrah.

This is a similar report from Mansur through another chain: Muhammad ibn Rafi, Yahya ibn Adam, and Mufaddal; and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Ibn Bashshar from Abd al-Rahman and Sufyan. The chain is Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah from Ghundar and Shubah; and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Ibn Bashshar from Muhammad ibn Jafar and Shubah, from Mansur, Abdullah ibn Murrah, and Ibn Umar.

Abu Hurairah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Do not make vows, for a vow cannot avert destiny in any way; it only draws something out of a miser.” Both chains report from Mansur through the same transmitters as Jarir narration: Muhammad ibn Rafi from Yahya ibn Adam and Mufaddal; and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Ibn Bashshar from Abd al-Rahman and Sufyan.

Abu Hurairah reported that the Prophet prohibited vows, saying: “They do not avert destiny; they only draw something out of a miser.” The chain is Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Ibn Bashshar, from Muhammad ibn Jafar, Shubah, al-Ala, his father, and Abu Hurairah.

Abu Hurairah reported that the Prophet said: “A vow does not bring a person anything that Allah has not decreed for him. Rather, a vow coincides with destiny and thereby brings out from a miser what he had not intended to give.”

This is the same report through Yaqub ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Qari and Abd al-Aziz al-Darawardi, both from Amr ibn Abi Amr, with the same chain and wording. The Prophet explained that a vow does not bring a person nearer to something Allah had not decreed for him. Rather, the vow coincides with destiny and causes a miser to give what he had not intended to give. The chain is Yahya ibn Ayyub, Qutaybah ibn Said, Ali ibn Hujr, Ismail ibn Jafar, Amr ibn Abi Amr, al-Araj, and Abu Hurairah.

This is a similar report through Qutaybah ibn Said, Yaqub ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Qari, and Abd al-Aziz al-Darawardi, from Amr ibn Abi Amr. It follows the same chain and wording as the preceding narration.

Imran ibn Husayn reported that Thaqif, allies of Banu Uqayl, captured two of the Prophet’s companions, while the companions captured a man of Banu Uqayl and took his camel, al-Adba. The Prophet passed the captive, who called, “Muhammad!” The Prophet came and asked what he needed. The man asked why he had been captured along with the famous she-camel. The Prophet replied that he had been taken because of the actions of his allies, Thaqif. The Prophet turned away, but the man called again and said, “I am a Muslim.” The Prophet replied, “Had you said that while you were still in control of your affairs, you would have fully succeeded.” The man called again, saying he was hungry and thirsty. The Prophet said, “That is your need,” and he was exchanged for the two captives. Imran then told of an Ansari woman who was captured and whose camel, al-Adba, was taken. One night she escaped her restraints and went among the camels. Each camel grunted as she approached, so she passed them until she reached al-Adba, which did not grunt. She mounted its hindquarters, urged it on, and escaped despite the people pursuing her. She vowed to Allah that if He saved her on it, she would sacrifice it. When she reached Madinah, people recognized it as the Messenger’s camel. She told them of her vow. The matter was brought to the Messenger, who said, “How badly she has repaid it! She vowed to Allah that if He saved her on it, she would sacrifice it. There is no fulfillment of a vow in disobedience, nor in something a person does not own.” Ibn Hujr’s version says: “There is no vow in disobedience to Allah.” The chain is Ismail ibn Ibrahim, Ayyub, Abu Qilabah, Abu al-Muhallab, and Imran ibn Husayn.

Anas reported that the Prophet saw an old man being supported as he walked between his two sons. He asked what was wrong. They said the man had vowed to walk. The Prophet said, “Allah has no need of this man punishing himself,” and ordered him to ride. The report has the same chain through Abu Qilabah and Imran ibn Husayn. Hammad version says al-Adba belonged to a man of Banu Uqayl and was a famous racing camel used in pilgrimage. It says the woman rode a docile, trained camel; al-Thaqafi version calls it trained.

Abu Hurairah reported that the Prophet caught up with an old man walking while leaning on his two sons. His sons said he had made a vow. The Prophet said, “Ride, old man. Allah has no need of you or your vow.” The chain is Yahya ibn Ayyub, Qutaybah, Ibn Hujr, Ismail ibn Jafar, Amr ibn Abi Amr, al-Araj, and Abu Hurairah.

This is the same report through Qutaybah ibn Said, Abd al-Aziz al-Darawardi, and Amr ibn Abi Amr. The Prophet asked the sons why the old man was being supported between them. They said he had vowed to walk. He ordered him to ride, explaining that Allah had no need for him to suffer for his vow. The chain includes Yahya ibn Ayyub, Qutaybah, Ibn Hujr, Ismail ibn Jafar, Amr ibn Abi Amr, al-Araj, and Abu Hurairah.
Uqbah ibn Amir said: “My sister vowed to walk barefoot to the House of Allah and asked me to seek the Messenger’s ruling for her. I asked him, and he said, ‘Let her walk and ride.’”

Uqbah ibn Amir al-Juhani reported the same ruling for his sister’s vow. This version does not mention that she vowed to go barefoot. It adds that Abu al-Khayr stayed constantly with Uqbah. Another chain from Muhammad ibn Hatim and Ibn Abi Khalaf through Rawh ibn Ubadah and Ibn Jurayj reports the same account.

Uqbah ibn Amir reported through Muhammad ibn Rafi, Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jurayj, Said ibn Abi Ayyub, Yazid ibn Abi Habib, and Abu al-Khayr that his sister made a vow to walk to the House of Allah. This is like the report of al-Mufaddal, except it does not mention that she was barefoot. It also adds that Abu al-Khayr remained with Uqbah. A second chain through Muhammad ibn Hatim, Ibn Abi Khalaf, Rawh ibn Ubadah, and Ibn Jurayj reports the same account.
